title: Aversion's family

segments.voice: Yesterday, greed's family: greed, wrong view and conceit. Your line: greed's family. Did you catch the scale coming out, better, equal or worse? Day one thousand seventy-six.

A text arrives from an old classmate. She got the job, the one both of them applied for. The reply goes out fast: congratulations, three exclamation points, a party emoji. And underneath the exclamation points, something small turns its face away. Yesterday's family leaned toward things. Today's family leans the other way. The Abhidhamma has a name for that turning away, and it gives it three relatives, one of which is a surprise.

The head of this family is dosa, aversion. It's the opposite lean from greed: not toward, but away. In the Abhidhamma it covers the whole range, from fury down to a mild ugh: irritation, dread, sulking, the small flinch at a voice in the next room. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha gives it three relatives that appear only in its company. Envy, issa: the mind that can't bear someone else's good fortune. Stinginess, macchariya: the mind that can't bear sharing its own. Look at those two side by side. Envy watches their plate. Stinginess guards mine. Both push something away, so the manual seats them with aversion, not with greed. The third relative is kukkucca, regret, or worry: brooding over a thing done that shouldn't have been, or a thing left undone that should have been. Regret can sound like conscience. But in this list, the stewing kind is a pushing against the past, aversion turned back on oneself. Seeing a mistake clearly and making amends is a different matter. What keeps this family fed? The Dhammapada answers near its start, in Max Müller's words: "'He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,'--in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease." Harbor is the telling word. A harbor is where boats are tied up and kept. Envy works the same way: one comparison, tied up and replayed. Regret too: one evening, docked and visited every night. The family doesn't need new reasons. It lives on the ones already kept. In a few days this path meets the factor the tradition sets against envy, gladness at someone else's good.
screen: `NOT TOWARD, BUT AWAY.` · `ENVY WATCHES THEIRS; STINGINESS GUARDS MINE.` · `REGRET PUSHES AT THE PAST.` · then, large: `HARBORED THOUGHTS KEEP IT FED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: notice one flicker of envy. Sit, and breathe. Then, gently, bring to mind someone who has something you'd like: a job, a home, an ease, a gift for something. Watch the very first moment. Is there a small tightening, a turning away? If there is, that's envy, and it's only a moment. Don't scold it. Feel where it sits. Then, if you can, add one plain thought: good for them. It doesn't have to be fully meant. Just see what happens to the tightness. The bell holds the time.
Aversion's family. Aversion, envy, stinginess and regret: four ways the mind pushes away. Today's word.
Your line: aversion's family. Today, when someone's good news lands, notice the first flicker before you reply. Then reply anyway, and see if it softens. Day one thousand seventy-six.

howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn aversion, envy, stinginess and regret as the hate-group of unwholesome factors, and in some Buddhist communities people meet envy by deliberately rejoicing in others' good fortune.

notes: Abhidhammattha Sangaha ch. 2: issa, macchariya and kukkucca arise only in the two hate-rooted cittas (and not necessarily together). Confirm the plain wording 'appear only in its company'.
Kukkucca is glossed as regret or worry, the brooding over what was done or left undone; the contrast with 'seeing a mistake clearly and making amends' is interpretive. Confirm it's fair.
The harbor wordplay is on Müller's English 'harbour', not on the Pali. It is offered as an image, not an etymology.
The forward reference to gladness (mudita) points at day 1081.
Avoided Dhammapada 5 to vary from earlier uses on this path.
